To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sepsis-induced changes in Ca2+i homeostasis are responsible for the generation of the inappropriate cellular responses during sepsis.

sepsis-related alterations in intracellular calcium (Ca(2+)i) homeostasis contribute to the generation of sepsis-induced inappropriate cellular responses, which include exaggerated hepatic acute phase protein (APP) response, insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, and suppressed T lymphocyte proliferation.
sepsis induces alterations in Ca2+ signaling and cellular responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the elucidation of the molecular basis of the sepsic-related alterations in the cellular Ca2+ homeostasis and the identification of the mechanisms by which these changes can affect the sepsis-induced cellular responses.
the role of Ca2+i homeostasis in sepsis-related cellular responses.
the elucidation of the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the sepsis-induced alterations in the cellular Ca2+i homeostasis and the resulting sepsis-induced inappropriate cellular responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sepsis-induced alterations in cellular Ca2+i homeostasis are the major contributors to the sepsis-mediated inappropriate cellular responses.
alterations in Ca2+i homeostasis are a major contributing factor for the inappropriate responses of the immune and endocrine systems in septic injury.
alterations in intracellular calcium homeostasis in sepsis are multifaceted and complex, and that they can affect a variety of cellular responses, some of which may be detrimental to the host.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

alterations in Ca2+ signaling and cellular responses during sepsis can be explained by the following: (1) an increase in the apparent basal [Ca 2+]i in hepatocytes, skeletal muscle cells, and T lymphocytes, (2) a decrease in TCR-mediated Ca2+i mobilizing in T lymphocytes, and (3) a decrease in insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation and glucose uptake in skeletal muscle cells.
sepsis-induced alterations in cellular responses are mediated by alterations in Ca2+i homeostasis.
the immune and endocrine agonists that are released during the septic response can affect cellular responses by altering intracellular Ca2+i homeostasis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sepsis-mediated alterations in Ca2+ signaling and cellular responses can be attributed to the actions of a number of sepsis-related mediators.
the immune and endocrine sepsis mediators can affect cellular functions via alterations in Ca2+i signaling.
the sepsis-induced alterations in cellular Ca2+i homeostasis can be a major factor in the development of the inappropriate sepsis-related cellular responses.
